# Activity Selection

## Summary

Given a set of activities with start and end times, choose the largest possible
number of them that do not overlap. Return the count.

## Constraints

- Activities arrive in arbitrary order and must be sorted by **end** time.
- An activity may start exactly when the previous one ends — touching endpoints
  do not count as an overlap.
- The list may be empty (answer: `0`).
- Zero-length activities (`[3, 3]`) are allowed.

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `[[1,3],[2,5],[4,6],[6,7],[5,9],[8,9]]` | `4` | `[1,3] [4,6] [6,7] [8,9]` |
| `[[1,2],[3,4],[5,6]]` | `3` | nothing overlaps |
| `[[1,10],[2,9],[3,8]]` | `1` | everything overlaps everything |
| `[[1,9],[2,3],[4,5]]` | `2` | the long activity loses to two short ones |

## Edge Cases

- Empty input — the starter solution indexes `activities[0]` before checking,
  so it crashes here. That is the first thing to fix when you write your own.
- A single activity.
- Identical activities, where only one can be chosen.
- Activities that touch at an endpoint (`[1,2]` and `[2,3]` are compatible).
- Input already sorted by start time, which is the ordering that tempts you into
  the wrong greedy choice.

## Complexity

- **Time:** `O(n log n)`, dominated by the sort; the scan afterwards is `O(n)`.
- **Space:** `O(1)` beyond the sort (`O(n)` if the sort is not in place).

## Why This Category

This is the textbook proof that a greedy choice can be optimal. Sorting by
earliest end time and always taking the first compatible activity works because
of an exchange argument: any optimal schedule can have its first activity
swapped for the earliest-ending one without reducing the count, and the argument
then repeats on the rest. Greedy problems live or die on whether such an
argument exists — the skill is testing your rule against a counterexample before
trusting it.

## Thought Process

- The three tempting rules — shortest duration, earliest start, fewest conflicts
  — all have counterexamples. Earliest end time is the one that survives, and
  the intuition is that it leaves the most room for whatever comes next.
- `[[1,9],[2,3],[4,5]]` is the counterexample to earliest-start: taking `[1,9]`
  first blocks two activities.
- Sort by end, then track only `lastEnd`. There is no need to keep the chosen
  set unless the problem asks for it.
- The complement of this problem — "minimum removals so nothing overlaps" — is
  the same algorithm subtracted from `n`.
